knownStaleness.problem: Names Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II. The reigning monarch is King Charles III, and the Oath was amended in June 2021 to add recognition of Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Metis peoples. Recorded at chapter grain until 2026-09-08, which forced volatile on all 38 questions in Rights and Responsibilities while the Oath is not in that chapter's pages at all — a flag firing on everything, which carries the same information as one firing on nothing. Both pages are listed because the extraction prints a page number after that page's text, so the Oath sits after marker 2 and is page 3 by that convention while the manifest records page 2; the wider span is the safe direction until the convention is settled. 2026-09-13: the flag still could not fire. applicableFlags needs the CHAPTER and the PAGE to match, and pages 2-3 fell inside no entry of chapters[] at all - the first was Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship at 11-15 - so a question citing this flag's pages was rejected for citing a page outside its chapter, and a question citing the chapter could never reach these pages. The Oath was uncitable and unflaggable at once. chapters[] now carries "The Oath of Citizenship" at 2-3, which is a heading the document really prints, and it is ADDED to affects rather than swapped in: nothing this flag covers today stops being covered.
knownStaleness.action: volatile: verify against the live canada.ca page, never against this file. upstream is still "unknown" here, so ADR-0016 section 2 puts a claim on pages 2-3 on row 1 and the volatile demand stands. knownStaleness.topic: Population shares and religious affiliation in Who We Are
knownStaleness.problem: The chapter's proportions are from the 2006 census era and the 2021 Census has moved all of them. The guide says First Nations are "about 65%" of Indigenous people (2021: 58.0%), that "about half" of First Nations people live on reserve (2021: 40.6% among status First Nations), and that "the great majority of Canadians identify as Christians" (2021: 53.3%, just over half). The last is the worst for a learning game: "No religion" is now 34.6%, larger than Catholic at 29.9%, so a question teaching the guide's framing punishes a learner who knows the current figure. Recorded at chapter grain for a few minutes on 2026-09-08, which forced volatile on all 46 questions in the chapter when three carry the shares — the same defect this register already had for the Oath, repeated by the same hand within the hour.
knownStaleness.action: volatile: never put one of these shares in an option or an explanation. The live page (who-are-canadians.html, Date modified 2025-08-08) still carries every one of them, so the modification date is not evidence of revision and re-fetching resolves nothing. Recorded here as prose first, which was the same defect ADR-0016 section 1 had already fixed: that sentence is a live check, and it has been transcribed into liveChecks[] where a gate can read it and where it expires. With it, Who We Are is on ADR-0016 section 2 row 2, so the volatile demand no longer fires on the fifteen questions that share pages 17, 18 and 21 with these shares and carry facts that will never move - treaty rights, the Royal Proclamation, residential schools, the 2008 apology, the meaning of "Inuit", Michif. bannedFromAnswers is the whole mitigation on row 2, and the clock that keeps it honest is liveChecks[].checkedAt, not a per-question re-fetch. Claim-level grain would still be finer than page grain, but it is no longer what this entry costs: page grain now over-reaches only into a term search, not into fifteen re-verifications.

knownStaleness.problem: Page 90 lists Russia among the G8. Russia was suspended in March 2014 and the group has met as the G7 ever since. Confirmed against the live page on 2026-09-09, Date modified 2025-04-11: it still names Russia, eleven years on.
knownStaleness.action: G7 is banned beside G8 deliberately: an option naming the G7 is right about the world and wrong about the document the exam is drawn from, so no answer may rest on the group's name in either direction. The flag stops at the G8 clause -- the same sentence's ranking claim is volatile's job, and folding it in would over-fire onto a usable proposition and repeat the grain defect this register keeps closing.

knownStaleness.action: Both the dead name and the current one are banned, for the reason G7 is banned beside G8: an option naming CUSMA is right about the world and wrong about the document the exam is drawn from. Recorded and not flagged: the same sentence's "over 444 million people and over $1 trillion in merchandise trade in 2008" is a 2008 figure printed as current. Nothing cites it and nothing should.

knownStaleness.topic: The 2008 trade and population figures in Canada's Economy
knownStaleness.problem: Page 90 prints "over 444 million people and over $1 trillion in merchandise trade in 2008" as a present-tense description of North American free trade. It is an eighteen-year-old magnitude in the same sentence as NAFTA, which was replaced by CUSMA on 2020-07-01, so the sentence is stale twice over for two different reasons. Confirmed against the live page (canadas-economy.html, Date modified 2025-04-11) on 2026-09-09: it still prints the same 2008 figures. Nothing in the bank cites them today. ADR-0028 sends an author onto this page's neighbours looking for propositions, and a number in a sentence is the most quotable thing on a short page, so this is recorded before it is needed rather than after.
knownStaleness.action: No option or explanation may rest on a trade volume or a population total from this page, and that includes a corrected one: a 2026 figure is right about the world and wrong about the document the exam is drawn from, which is the reason G7 is banned beside G8 in the entry above. The teachable propositions in this sentence are the DATES and the PARTNERS -- free trade with the United States in 1988, Mexico joining in 1994 -- and both are already claimed. Ask about those or about nothing here.

knownStaleness.problem: Every population count in the chapter is a 2011-era figure printed in the present tense. Page 94: "Canada has a population of about 34 million people" (2021 Census 36,991,981, and past 41 million since). Page 98: "Nearly eight million people live in Quebec". Page 99: "At more than 12 million, the people of Ontario". Page 102: British Columbia "with a population of four million". Page 103: the three territories "have a population of only 100,000". Page 104: Yellowknife "(population 20,000)" and, on page 100, St. Boniface's Francophone community "at 45,000". Confirmed against the live page (canadas-regions.html, Date modified 2025-05-12) on 2026-09-10: every figure is still there, unchanged.
knownStaleness.action: No option and no explanation may state a population from this chapter, and that includes a CORRECTED one - a 2026 count is right about the world and wrong about the document the exam is drawn from, which is the reason G7 is banned beside G8 on page 90. The terms above are the literal spellings the guide uses; the rule is wider than the list and a figure written with a non-breaking space or spelled out ("thirty-four million") evades the matcher without evading the rule. What the chapter offers instead, and what the fourteen shipped economy questions grade, is which province produces WHAT - resources, industries, ports and capitals - none of which is a magnitude.

knownStaleness.topic: Shares, proportions and rankings in Canada's Regions
knownStaleness.problem: The chapter's proportions are census-era or output-share figures that have moved, and its rankings are point-in-time. Page 94: Ottawa is "Canada's fourth largest metropolitan area". Page 98: Quebec's "More than three-quarters speak French as their first language" (2021 Census 74.8% mother tongue, now under three-quarters) and "Ontario and Quebec produce more than three-quarters of all Canadian manufactured goods". Page 99: Ontario is "more than one-third of Canadians". Page 100: Manitoba's "14% reporting Ukrainian origins" and "largest Aboriginal population of any province, at over 15%" (2021: 18.1%, and largest by SHARE only - Ontario is largest by count), and Saskatchewan's "40% of the arable land in Canada". Page 102: "About one-half of all the goods produced in B.C. are forestry products" and "approximately 600 provincial parks". Confirmed against the live page on 2026-09-10: all still present, unchanged.
knownStaleness.action: Ask which province produces a thing, never what share of it. "Ontario and Quebec make most of Canada's manufactured goods" is durable and is what eco-25 grades; "more than three-quarters" is not, and sits in that question's source.quote only, where nothing a player reads can inherit it. Two entries here are deliberately narrower than the stale fact and this says so rather than letting the list imply coverage: "one-third" is NOT banned, because the territories holding one-third of Canada's land mass is geography and cannot move, and Ontario at more than one-third of Canadians is still true; and bare "half" and "moitié" are not banned because they are ordinary words whose every use would fire. A share that slips through in those spellings is caught by the verifier reading the chapter, not here. Page 104 added 2026-09-13. It carries Nunavut's "about 85% Inuit" and the Northwest Territories' "more than half the population is Aboriginal", which are exactly this flag's shape and were outside it. Nothing ships on either -- an author dropped both on content-review grounds -- but that was judgement rather than the gate, and the next author on that page would have had no warning. Page 103 stays out deliberately: its one-third of Canada's land mass is geography this register declines to ban.

knownStaleness.topic: The Court of Queen's Bench in The Justice System
knownStaleness.problem: Page 76 says that in most provinces the trial court is "sometimes called the Court of Queen’s Bench or the Supreme Court". Since the 2022 accession, that court is the Court of King's Bench in at least four provinces. Each is sourced from the province's own court or government site, fetched 2026-09-13. ALBERTA: albertacourts.ca/kb/home is headed "Court of King's Bench of Alberta" and says "The Court of King's Bench is the Superior Trial Court for the Province". SASKATCHEWAN: sasklawcourts.ca/court-of-kings-bench/ carries a notice dated Sep 8, 2022: "With the death of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, and the succession of His Majesty King Charles III, the Court of Queen’s Bench becomes the Court of King’s Bench. The name change takes effect immediately." MANITOBA: manitobacourts.mb.ca shows "Home > Court of King's Bench > News and Announcements" and a notice posted June 30, 2026 on "Amendment of Court of King's Bench Rules". Its URLs still read /court-of-queens-bench/, and /court-of-kings-bench/ returns 404. The province's statutes site, web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/c280e.php, lists "Court of King's Bench: civil rules". NEW BRUNSWICK: courtsnb-coursnb.ca/content/cour/en/kings-bench.html is headed "The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick", and its French page, banc-du-roi.html, names the "Cour du Banc du Roi du Nouveau-Brunswick", once with a non-breaking space inside "Banc du Roi". NOT SOURCED, and not claimed: whether any other province or territory had or has a Court of Queen's Bench or King's Bench; how and when Alberta, Manitoba and New Brunswick made the change (only Saskatchewan's date and wording come from its own page); and whether any province still calls its trial court the Supreme Court, which is the other half of the sentence. The live English chapter (Date modified 2017-12-21) and the live French chapter (Date de modification 2023-09-07, « Cour du Banc de la Reine ») both still print the pre-accession name; see liveChecks for The Justice System, 2026-09-13. One question put "the Court of Queen's Bench" in a correct answer during the week of 2026-09-13, and only a verifier's reading caught it, because no flag covered this page.
knownStaleness.action: Both the old name and the new one are banned in both languages, for the reason G7 is banned beside G8. An option naming the Court of King's Bench is right about Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and New Brunswick and wrong about the document the exam is drawn from, and one naming the Court of Queen's Bench is the reverse. The teachable part of the sentence cannot move: most provinces have an appeal court and a trial court. That is what jus-17 grades, and jus-37 grades the trial court's other name, the Supreme Court of the province. Ask about those, or about neither court's name. HOW THE LIST IS BUILT. mentionsTerm lowercases and then matches the literal string. It normalises neither apostrophes nor spaces, so each explicit form is listed once per apostrophe code point an author or a paste can produce: U+0027, U+2019, U+2018, U+02BC, U+0060, U+00B4, U+2032 and U+FF07, plus the form with no apostrophe. That list is still open-ended, and a probe of the matcher on 2026-09-13 showed an explicit term also misses a non-breaking space ("King’s\u00A0Bench", "Banc\u00A0du Roi") and a doubled space. New Brunswick's own French page prints the non-breaking form. U+02BC also counts as a letter under \p{L}, so it is not a word boundary. The bare whole words "Bench" and "Banc" are therefore the real catch-all and are deliberate. They match every spacing and apostrophe variant of all four names and do not match "benches" or "bancs" (the page's "Jury benches" caption). They WILL fire on "a judge on the bench" or « le banc des accusés » in any option or explanation citing page 76. That is the accepted direction, and the fix is to refine this entry, not to argue with the gate. "QB" and "KB" are listed because Manitoba's court site writes "KB Notices". "Supreme Court" is NOT banned: it is also the name of the country's highest court, which jus-15 grades on this page and jus-37 uses as a distractor. As before, the rule is wider than the list, and a verifier reading page 76 still has to catch anything the matcher cannot. source.quote and verification.evidence are not searched, so jus-17's and jus-37's verbatim quote of the stale sentence is untouched by this flag.

liveChecks.consequence: Fetched first-hand as raw HTML, not through a summarising reader. The text of <main> was extracted and compared word by word, with difflib over word sequences, against pages 75-77 of the cached extraction (extractedTextSha256 fd51046981...).
